method_card.title: Titrations and Molar Concentrations
steps: Convert every volume from cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000.
Find the moles of the solution you know: moles = concentration × volume.
Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to get the moles of the unknown.
Find the unknown's concentration (moles ÷ volume) or mass (moles × Mr).
method_card.content:
Every titration calculation is the same three moves: moles of what you know, the mole ratio, then the unknown.

Volumes arrive in cm³. Divide by 1000 to reach dm³ before using \(c = \frac{n}{V}\). Check the ratio in the balanced equation, as it is not always 1:1. If a mass is given, start with \(n = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\). If a volumetric flask is used, the concentration is the same in the small sample and the whole flask, so scale the moles up by the volumes.
method_card.example:
Solve: 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ HCl neutralises 25.0 cm³ of NaOH (ratio 1:1).

Moles HCl = 0.125 × 0.02 = 0.0025. Ratio 1:1, so 0.0025 mol NaOH. Concentration = 0.0025 ÷ 0.025 = 0.1 mol/dm³.

exam_context.frequency: High: titration calculations appear almost every year in Separate Chemistry

gold.display: 2.0 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved in water and made up to 200 cm³ in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl. The titre is 31.25 cm³. The equation is: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: First find moles NaOH = 2/40 = 0.05 mol. Conc in flask = 0.05/0.2 = 0.25 mol/dm³. Moles in 25cm³ = 0.25 × 0.025 = 0.00625. Conc HCl = 0.00625/0.03125 = 0.2 mol/dm³.
The 200 cm³ is the total flask volume. You only use 25.0 cm³ in the titration.

gold.hint: Find moles of NaOH, its concentration in the flask, then work through the titration to the HCl.

guided_steps.say: Start from the solid NaOH, find the flask concentration, then work the titration through to the HCl.
The ratio NaOH : HCl is 1 : 1, so moles HCl = 0.00625.

guided_steps.hint: HCl moles divided by the titre volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the HCl moles, so 0.2 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl, and the titre is 25.0 cm³. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2. You need double the moles of HCl.

gold.hint: Work out Mr and moles first, then the flask concentration, then the titration chain.

guided_steps.say: Find the Mr and moles of the solid, the flask concentration, then the titration chain with a 1:2 ratio.

guided_steps.pre: The ratio Na₂CO₃ : HCl is 1 : 2, so moles HCl = 0.005 × 2 =
The titre is also 25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³. concentration HCl = 0.01 ÷ 0.025 =
guided_steps.hint: HCl moles divided by the titre volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the HCl moles, so 0.4 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of hydrogen chloride (HCl) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.5 mol/dm³ solution. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
gold.hint: Moles first (concentration × volume in dm³), then mass = moles × Mr.

guided_steps.say: Find the moles from concentration and volume, then turn moles into mass with the Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values for H and Cl.
The second decimal is a 6, so round the first decimal up.
guided_steps.done: So the mass of HCl is 4.6 g.

gold.display: A student dissolves some KOH in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. A 25.0 cm³ sample is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl. KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the mass of KOH originally dissolved. (Ar: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles HCl = 0.1 × 0.02 = 0.002. 1:1 ratio, so moles KOH in 25cm³ = 0.002. Conc KOH = 0.002/0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm³. Total moles in 500cm³ = 0.08 × 0.5 = 0.04 mol. Mr KOH = 56. Mass = 0.04 × 56 = 2.24 g.
The titration uses 25 cm³ from a 500 cm³ flask. Scale up: total moles = conc × 0.5 dm³.

gold.hint: The titration gives the concentration in the flask. Scale up to 500 cm³, then find the mass.

guided_steps.say: The titration gives the concentration in the flask. Scale it up to the whole 500 cm³, then find the mass.
The ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of KOH in the sample = 0.002.

guided_steps.hint: Sample moles divided by sample volume.
Add the Ar values for K, O and H.
Mass divided by Mr gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the total moles, so 2.24 g is right.

gold.display: A student dissolves some NaOH in water and makes 250 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ HNO₃. NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of NaOH dissolved. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles HNO₃ = 0.2 × 0.02 = 0.004. 1:1 ratio. Conc NaOH = 0.004/0.025 = 0.16 mol/dm³. Total moles = 0.16 × 0.25 = 0.04. Mr NaOH = 40. Mass = 0.04 × 40 = 1.6 g.
You titrated 25 cm³ from a 250 cm³ flask. Multiply the sample moles by 10 to get the total.

gold.hint: Find the concentration from the titration, scale to 250 cm³, then mass = moles × Mr.

guided_steps.say: The titration gives the flask concentration. Scale up to 250 cm³, then find the mass.
The ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of NaOH in the sample = 0.004.

guided_steps.hint: Sample moles divided by sample volume.
Add the Ar values for Na, O and H.
Mass divided by Mr gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the total moles, so 1.6 g is right.

gold.display: A student dissolves Na₂CO₃ in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 12.5 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the mass of Na₂CO₃ originally dissolved. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
gold.hint: The titration gives the flask concentration. Scale to 500 cm³, then multiply by Mr.

guided_steps.say: The titration gives the flask concentration. Scale up to 500 cm³, then find the mass.
The ratio Na₂CO₃ : H₂SO₄ is 1 : 1, so moles of Na₂CO₃ in the sample = 0.00125.

guided_steps.hint: Sample moles divided by sample volume.
Mass divided by Mr gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the total moles, so 2.65 g is right.

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.1 mol/dm³. Calculate the number of moles in 25.0 cm³ of this solution.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm³ to dm³ first: 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³. Then moles = 0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol.
Did you divide the volume by 1000? 25 cm³ = 0.025 dm³, not 25 dm³.

bronze.hint: Turn the volume into dm³ first, then multiply by the concentration.

guided_steps.say: Concentration links moles and volume: \(n = c \times V\). But the volume has to be in dm³ first.

guided_steps.hint: Moles divided by volume gives the concentration back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the concentration we started with, so 0.0025 mol is right.

bronze.display: 0.5 mol of a solute is dissolved in 0.25 dm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2 mol/dm³. Don't multiply.

bronze.hint: Concentration is moles divided by volume. The volume is already in dm³.

guided_steps.say: Concentration is moles over volume: \(c = \frac{n}{V}\). The volume is already in dm³, so nothing to convert.

guided_steps.pre: Which number is the volume, in dm³? V =
guided_steps.hint: Read it from the question: 0.25 dm³.
Divide the moles by the volume.
Concentration times volume should give the moles back.
guided_steps.done: That is the moles we were given, so 2 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³. What volume (in dm³) is needed to contain 0.2 mol?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: volume = moles ÷ concentration = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = 0.4 dm³.

guided_steps.say: This asks for a volume, so rearrange: \(V = \frac{n}{c}\).

guided_steps.pre: Which number is the moles? n =
guided_steps.hint: Read it from the question: 0.2 mol.
Concentration times volume should give the moles.
guided_steps.done: That gives the 0.2 mol we needed, so 0.4 dm³ is right.

bronze.display: 4.0 g of NaOH is dissolved in 500 cm³ of water. Calculate the number of moles of NaOH. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol.

bronze.hint: Work out the Mr, then moles = mass ÷ Mr. The volume is not needed here.

guided_steps.say: A mass, so start with \(n = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\). The 500 cm³ of water is not needed for the moles.

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values for Na, O and H.
Moles times Mr should give the mass back.
guided_steps.done: That is the 4.0 g we started with, so 0.1 mol is right.

bronze.display: A solution contains 0.15 mol of solute in 500 cm³. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert volume first: 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Concentration = 0.15 ÷ 0.5 = 0.3 mol/dm³.

bronze.hint: Change 500 cm³ into dm³, then divide the moles by it.

guided_steps.say: Concentration is moles over volume: \(c = \frac{n}{V}\), with the volume in dm³.

guided_steps.hint: Moles divided by volume in dm³.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.15 mol, so 0.3 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 100 cm³ of a 0.25 mol/dm³ solution.
bronze.hint: Change 100 cm³ into dm³, then multiply by the concentration.

guided_steps.say: \(n = c \times V\), with the volume in dm³.

guided_steps.hint: Moles divided by volume gives the concentration.
guided_steps.done: Back to the concentration, so 0.025 mol is right.

misconceptions.message: Divide by 1000, not 100. 50 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.05 dm³.

bronze.hint: One dm³ is 1000 cm³, so divide by 1000.

guided_steps.say: A pure unit conversion. Remember how many cm³ fit in one dm³.

guided_steps.hint: A dm³ is a litre, which is 1000 cm³.
Multiplying by 1000 should give the cm³ back.
guided_steps.done: Back to 50 cm³, so 0.05 dm³ is right.

bronze.display: 2.0 g of HCl is dissolved in water. Calculate the number of moles. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
bronze.hint: Work out the Mr of HCl, then divide the mass by it.

guided_steps.say: A mass, so \(n = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\).

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values for H and Cl.
Mass divided by Mr, rounded to 3 significant figures.
Moles times Mr should come back to about 2 g.
guided_steps.done: Close to the 2.0 g we started with, so 0.0548 mol is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ HCl. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio, then \(c = \frac{n}{V}\)

misconceptions.message: Convert volumes to dm³: 20.0 cm³ = 0.02 dm³, 25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³. Moles HCl = 0.125 × 0.02 = 0.0025. Ratio 1:1, so moles NaOH = 0.0025. Conc = 0.0025 ÷ 0.025 = 0.1 mol/dm³.
Use the NaOH volume (25.0 cm³) for the final step, not the HCl volume.

silver.hint: Moles of HCl first, then a 1:1 ratio, then divide by the NaOH volume.

guided_steps.say: Three moves: moles of the acid you know, the mole ratio, then the concentration of the base.
The ratio HCl : NaOH is 1 : 1, so moles of NaOH = 0.0025 as well.

guided_steps.hint: Moles of NaOH divided by its own volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the NaOH moles, so 0.1 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 1:2 (H₂SO₄ : NaOH). Moles NaOH = 0.2 × 0.025 = 0.005. Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.005 ÷ 2 = 0.0025. Conc = 0.0025 ÷ 0.02 = 0.125 mol/dm³.
Don't forget the 2:1 ratio. You need half as many moles of H₂SO₄ as NaOH.

silver.hint: Find moles of NaOH, halve for the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the acid volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles of the base, then halve for the 1:2 ratio, then the acid's concentration.

guided_steps.pre: The ratio H₂SO₄ : NaOH is 1 : 2, so moles H₂SO₄ = 0.005 ÷ 2 =
guided_steps.hint: Half as much acid as base.
Acid moles divided by acid volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the acid moles, so 0.125 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.15 mol/dm³ HCl is neutralised by 18.75 cm³ of NaOH. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Use the NaOH volume for the final step. Moles HCl = 0.15 × 0.025 = 0.00375. Ratio 1:1. Conc NaOH = 0.00375 ÷ 0.01875 = 0.2 mol/dm³.

silver.hint: Moles of HCl, 1:1 ratio, then divide by the NaOH volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles of the acid, 1:1 ratio, then divide by the base volume.
The ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of NaOH = 0.00375.

guided_steps.hint: Base moles divided by base volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the moles, so 0.2 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ Ca(OH)₂ is neutralised by 10.0 cm³ of HCl. The equation is: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: The equation shows 2 moles of HCl per mole of Ca(OH)₂, so double the moles.

silver.hint: Moles of Ca(OH)₂, double for the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the HCl volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles of the base, double for the 1:2 ratio, then the acid concentration.

guided_steps.pre: The ratio Ca(OH)₂ : HCl is 1 : 2, so moles HCl = 0.0025 × 2 =
guided_steps.hint: Twice as much acid as base.
Acid moles divided by acid volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the acid moles, so 0.5 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of HNO₃. The equation is: KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HNO₃ in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Moles KOH = 0.2 × 0.025 = 0.005. Ratio 1:1. Conc HNO₃ = 0.005 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.4 mol/dm³. Use the HNO₃ volume (12.5 cm³) in the final step.

silver.hint: Moles of KOH, 1:1 ratio, then divide by the HNO₃ volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles of the base, 1:1 ratio, then divide by the acid volume.
The ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of HNO₃ = 0.005.

guided_steps.hint: Acid moles divided by acid volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the moles, so 0.4 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by 25.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: Two moles of KOH react with one mole of H₂SO₄. Halve the moles of KOH.

silver.hint: Moles of KOH, halve for the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the acid volume.

guided_steps.say: Moles of the base, halve for the 1:2 ratio, then the acid concentration.

guided_steps.pre: The ratio H₂SO₄ : KOH is 1 : 2, so moles H₂SO₄ = 0.0125 ÷ 2 =
guided_steps.hint: Half as much acid as base.
Acid moles divided by acid volume.
Concentration times volume gives the moles back.
guided_steps.done: Back to the acid moles, so 0.25 mol/dm³ is right.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One formula, one step: convert the volume to dm³ if needed, then use moles = concentration × volume, or rearrange it for whatever is missing.
problem_bank.silver_description: A full titration: moles of the solution you know, the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then the concentration of the one you do not know.
problem_bank.gold_description: Multi-step: a mass or a volumetric flask, scaling a small sample up to the whole flask, and finishing with mass from moles.

The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

bronze.title: Bronze: one formula, right units
steps: Concentration links three things: moles, volume in dm³, and concentration in mol/dm³. Use \(c = \frac{n}{V}\), or rearrange it for whatever is missing.
Volumes in these questions often come in cm³. Divide by 1000 to get dm³ BEFORE you substitute. This is the step that catches most people out.
If you are given a mass, turn it into moles first with \(n = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\).

example.question: Calculate the number of moles in 50 cm³ of a 0.4 mol/dm³ solution.

silver.title: Silver: the three-step titration
steps: Step one: find the moles of the solution you fully know, using \(n = c \times V\) with the volume in dm³.
Step two: read the mole ratio from the balanced equation. It is often 1:1, but acids like H₂SO₄ and bases like Ca(OH)₂ make it 1:2.
Step three: divide those moles by the other solution's volume in dm³ to get its concentration.

example.question: 25.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl neutralises 20.0 cm³ of NaOH. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Find the NaOH concentration.

gold.title: Gold: flasks, scaling and mass
steps: A volumetric flask holds a big volume (say 250 cm³), but you titrate only a small sample (say 25.0 cm³). The concentration is the same in both.
Find the concentration from the titration, then scale to the whole flask: total moles = concentration × flask volume in dm³.
If the question wants a mass, finish with mass = moles × Mr. If it gives a mass, start with moles = mass ÷ Mr.

example.question: 4.0 g of NaOH (Mr 40) is made up to 200 cm³. Find the concentration in mol/dm³.

opener.label: Before any chemistry
opener.display: A 2 litre jug of squash is made with 4 scoops of powder.

steps.say: No chemistry yet, just share it out.
steps.pre: How many scoops are in each litre?

steps.say: That is concentration: amount shared over volume. In chemistry the amount is counted in moles and the volume in dm³, and a dm³ is just a litre.
steps.pre: You pour out half a litre. How many scoops come with it?
steps.hint: Each litre holds 2 scoops, and you took half a litre.

steps.say: That second move is moles = concentration × volume. A titration just does these two moves twice: once for the solution you know, once for the one you are after. One habit to build: chemistry gives volumes in cm³, so divide by 1000 to get dm³ first.

bronze.label: Together: your first one
bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 250 cm³, then in 500 cm³, of a 0.2 mol/dm³ solution.

steps.say: Same equation each time: \(n = c \times V\), volume in dm³.

steps.done: Double the volume, double the moles, and the concentration never changed.

steps.pre: Ratio H₂SO₄ : NaOH = 1 : 2, so moles H₂SO₄ = 0.0025 ÷ 2 =
steps.hint: Half as much acid as base.
Acid moles divided by acid volume.
steps.done: The ratio step is the whole point of silver. That was it.

steps.say: The new move: a sample taken from a bigger flask. Find the flask concentration, then titrate the sample.

steps.pre: moles NaOH in the 25.0 cm³ sample = 0.8 × 0.025 =
steps.hint: Flask concentration times sample volume (0.025 dm³).

steps.pre: Ratio 1 : 1, and the titre is 40.0 cm³ = 0.04 dm³. concentration HCl = 0.02 ÷ 0.04 =
steps.hint: HCl moles divided by the titre volume.
